definition: The complex vector space with an inner product in which quantum states live; for n qubits it has dimension 2ⁿ.
A matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose. Its eigenvalues are real, so it can represent an observable or a Hamiltonian.
A matrix whose conjugate transpose is its inverse. Unitaries preserve inner products; time evolution and quantum gates are unitary.
Every Hermitian matrix can be written as V diag(λ) V† with real eigenvalues λ and an orthonormal eigenbasis V.
[A, B] = AB − BA. It vanishes exactly when A and B commute; non-zero commutators give uncertainty relations and Trotter error.
The matrix form of the tensor product: an mn × mn block matrix whose blocks are A_ij B. It combines states and operators of separate systems.
A column vector |ψ⟩ representing a quantum state in Dirac notation.
The conjugate transpose ⟨ψ| of a ket; a bra and a ket together give an inner product ⟨φ|ψ⟩.
The bra-ket notation for quantum states and operators: |ψ⟩ for states, ⟨φ|ψ⟩ for inner products, |ψ⟩⟨φ| for outer products.
A linear combination of basis states with complex amplitudes. Unlike a random mixture, it has definite relative phases that other measurements can detect.
A complex coefficient of a state in some basis; its squared modulus is the probability of that outcome.
An overall factor e^{iγ} on a state. It changes no measurement outcome, so states differing only by it are physically identical.
A phase between components of a superposition. Unlike a global phase it is measurable, though not by measuring in the basis it sits in.
Measuring |ψ⟩ in an orthonormal basis gives outcome k with probability |⟨e_k|ψ⟩|².
After a measurement the state is replaced by the (normalised) projection onto the observed outcome.
One run of a quantum experiment ending in a measurement; expectation values are estimated by averaging many shots.
A Hermitian operator representing a measurable quantity; its eigenvalues are the possible measurement results.
The average result of measuring an observable A on many copies of a state: ⟨A⟩ = ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩, or Tr(Aρ) for a density matrix.
For any state, σ_A σ_B ≥ |⟨[A, B]⟩|/2 (Robertson). Non-commuting observables cannot both be sharp.
A two-level quantum system with basis states |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The unit sphere on which every pure qubit state sits, with coordinates (⟨X⟩, ⟨Y⟩, ⟨Z⟩). Mixed states fill its interior, the Bloch ball.
The vector (⟨X⟩, ⟨Y⟩, ⟨Z⟩) of a qubit state; length 1 for pure states, less for mixed ones.
The three 2 × 2 matrices X, Y and Z: Hermitian, unitary, squaring to the identity and pairwise anticommuting.
A tensor product of one Pauli matrix or identity per qubit; the 4ⁿ strings form a basis for operators on n qubits.
R_P(θ) = exp(−iθP/2): a rotation of the Bloch sphere by θ about the axis of the Pauli P.
The single-qubit gate (X + Z)/√2, which exchanges the Z and X bases.
The controlled-NOT gate: flips the target qubit when the control is |1⟩. With single-qubit rotations it is universal.
One of four maximally entangled two-qubit states, such as (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.
Approximating exp(−i(A+B)t) by repeating short steps exp(−iAt/r)exp(−iBt/r); the error shrinks as the steps get shorter.
The Hermitian operator for a system's energy; it generates time evolution through U(t) = exp(−iHt).
i d|ψ⟩/dt = H|ψ⟩ (with ħ = 1), whose solution is |ψ(t)⟩ = exp(−iHt)|ψ(0)⟩.
An eigenvector of the Hamiltonian; under time evolution it only acquires a phase, so it is stationary.
Rotation of a spin's Bloch vector about the field axis; for H = hZ the angular frequency is 2h.
Periodic population transfer in a driven two-level system; on resonance the population swings fully between |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The description in which observables evolve, A(t) = U†AU, while the state stays fixed; it gives the same predictions as the Schrödinger picture.
An observable that commutes with the Hamiltonian; its probability distribution never changes under the evolution.
A block of the state space labelled by the value of a conserved quantity; the dynamics never connects different blocks.
The oscillator operator a with a|n⟩ = √n|n−1⟩; its adjoint a† is the creation operator, and [a, a†] = 1.
A state of definite quanta number |n⟩ of an oscillator mode, eigenstate of a†a.
An eigenstate of the annihilation operator, a|α⟩ = α|α⟩: Poisson photon numbers with mean |α|² and minimum quadrature noise.
The oscillator's position-like x = (a + a†)/√2 or momentum-like p = i(a† − a)/√2 operators, measured by homodyne detection.
A correlation of a multi-part pure state that cannot be written as a product of states of the parts.
Writing a two-party pure state as Σ λ_k |a_k⟩|b_k⟩ with orthonormal bases on each side; the number of non-zero λ_k is the Schmidt rank.
The operation that discards part of a composite system, leaving the reduced density matrix of the rest.
The density matrix of a subsystem, obtained by the partial trace; it reproduces every measurement on that subsystem.
The von Neumann entropy of either half of a pure bipartite state: 0 for a product, 1 bit for a Bell pair.
ρ = Σ p_j |ψ_j⟩⟨ψ_j|: the description of a possibly mixed state, Hermitian, positive and of trace 1, with ⟨A⟩ = Tr(Aρ).
A state that is not a single pure vector: a statistical mixture, or part of a larger entangled system. Its Bloch vector is shorter than 1.
Tr ρ², equal to 1 for pure states and down to 1/d for the maximally mixed state.
The density matrix I/d: every outcome equally likely in every basis, the centre of the Bloch ball.
The spin chain H = −J Σ Z_i Z_{i+1} − h Σ X_i, with a quantum phase transition at h = J.
A mapping of a one-dimensional chain of spins onto fermions; nearest-neighbour XY and transverse-field Ising chains become free fermions.

The complete description of a quantum system: a unit vector |ψ⟩ in Hilbert space (up to a global phase), or a density matrix when the state is mixed. Every prediction about measurements follows from it.
⟨φ|ψ⟩, the complex number comparing two states: the sum of φ's conjugated components times ψ's. |⟨φ|ψ⟩|² is the probability that a system in |ψ⟩ is found in |φ⟩; zero means the states are orthogonal.
The length of a vector, ‖ψ‖ = √⟨ψ|ψ⟩. Physical states are normalised to length 1 so their Born-rule probabilities add up to 1.
A set of unit vectors that are pairwise orthogonal and span the space. The possible outcomes of a measurement form one, and any state is a unique combination of its vectors.
The basis |0⟩, |1⟩ for one qubit and the bit strings |00…0⟩ to |11…1⟩ for n qubits: the eigenbasis of the Z operators and the basis hardware measures in by default.

The orthonormal basis whose vectors are a measurement's outcomes. Hardware measures in the computational basis, so measuring in another basis means rotating the state first (a Hadamard turns an X measurement into a Z measurement).
A number λ with A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩ for some nonzero vector |v⟩. For an observable the eigenvalues are the possible measurement results, and for a Hamiltonian they are the energies.
A nonzero vector that a matrix only rescales, A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩. An eigenstate of an observable gives that observable's value with certainty.
An orthonormal basis made of a matrix's eigenvectors. Every Hermitian or unitary matrix has one, and in it the matrix is diagonal.
The set of an operator's eigenvalues. An observable's spectrum lists its possible outcomes; a Hamiltonian's spectrum lists the allowed energies.
When two or more independent eigenvectors share one eigenvalue. Measuring a degenerate outcome does not single out a vector, only the subspace (eigenspace) it spans.
A†, the matrix transposed with every entry complex-conjugated. It turns a ket into its bra, and defines Hermitian (A† = A) and unitary (U†U = I) matrices.
|ψ⟩⟨φ|, a ket times a bra, which is a matrix rather than a number. |ψ⟩⟨ψ| is the projector onto |ψ⟩ and the density matrix of the pure state |ψ⟩.
An operator P with P² = P = P†. It keeps the part of a vector inside one subspace and removes the rest; measurement outcomes correspond to projectors onto eigenspaces.
The textbook measurement: outcome k occurs with probability ⟨ψ|P_k|ψ⟩ for projectors P_k that sum to the identity, and the state jumps to the normalised P_k|ψ⟩.
Tr A, the sum of a matrix's diagonal entries, which equals the sum of its eigenvalues. A density matrix has trace 1, and Tr(ρA) is the expectation value of A.
e^A = I + A + A²/2! + …, computed in practice by diagonalising A and exponentiating its eigenvalues. e^(−iHt) is how a Hamiltonian becomes a unitary.
U(t) = e^(−iHt/ħ), the unitary that carries a state from time 0 to time t under a time-independent Hamiltonian: |ψ(t)⟩ = U(t)|ψ(0)⟩.
How an isolated system changes in time: by a unitary operator, so norms, inner products and purity are preserved and the evolution can always be undone.
The constant ħ ≈ 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s that converts energy into angular frequency, E = ħω. Theory usually sets ħ = 1, so energies and frequencies are measured in the same units.
The eigenstate of a Hamiltonian with the lowest energy.
Any energy eigenstate above the ground state; for a qubit, usually |1⟩.
One of the allowed energies of a system, an eigenvalue of its Hamiltonian. Differences between levels set the frequencies the system responds to.
In quantum dynamics, driving a transition at the frequency matching the gap between two energy levels; at resonance a Rabi oscillation swings the full population between them.
The difference Δ between a drive's frequency and a transition's frequency. A detuned drive gives faster but incomplete Rabi oscillations, of amplitude Ω²/(Ω² + Δ²).
The usual bookkeeping in which states evolve in time and operators stay fixed. It gives the same predictions as the Heisenberg picture.
Observables whose operators commute. They share an eigenbasis, so they can be measured together, from the same shots, without disturbing each other.
Two operators anticommute when AB = −BA, i.e. their anticommutator {A, B} = AB + BA is zero. Different Pauli matrices anticommute.
In quantum mechanics, the spread of an observable's outcomes in a state: ⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩². It is zero exactly when the state is an eigenstate of A.

The short list the theory rests on: states are unit vectors in a Hilbert space, observables are Hermitian operators, outcome probabilities follow the Born rule, measurement updates the state, closed systems evolve unitarily, and composite systems combine by tensor product.
No physical process can copy an unknown quantum state. It is why a quantum state cannot be measured many times from one copy, and so why expectation values need many runs.
A computation written as a sequence of quantum gates on qubit wires, read left to right, usually ending in measurements.
A unitary operation on a few qubits, the quantum counterpart of a logic gate. Unlike most classical gates it is reversible.
A small set of gates, for example arbitrary single-qubit rotations plus CNOT, whose products can approximate any unitary to any accuracy.
A single-qubit gate that leaves |0⟩ alone and multiplies |1⟩ by a phase (i for the S gate, e^(iφ) in general): a rotation about the Z axis up to a global phase.
A two-qubit gate that applies an operation to a target qubit only when a control qubit is |1⟩. CNOT and controlled-Z are the common examples, and either one can create entanglement.
The two-qubit gate that exchanges the states of two qubits, |ab⟩ → |ba⟩. It takes three CNOTs.
A system made of parts, such as several qubits. Its Hilbert space is the tensor product of the parts' spaces, so its dimension is the product of theirs.
An operator that acts on only one part of a composite system, written A ⊗ I. Its expectation value depends only on that part's reduced state.
A state of a composite system that factorises, |ψ⟩ = |a⟩ ⊗ |b⟩: each part has a definite state of its own and there is no entanglement.
A mixed state that is a probabilistic mixture of product states. A state that is not separable is entangled.
A state that can be written as a single vector |ψ⟩; its density matrix |ψ⟩⟨ψ| has purity 1.
Classical uncertainty about which pure state was prepared: |ψ_i⟩ with probability p_i, described by ρ = Σ p_i |ψ_i⟩⟨ψ_i|. Unlike a superposition, it cannot interfere.
The off-diagonal entries of a density matrix in a chosen basis. They carry the relative phases that make interference possible; a statistical mixture in that basis has none.
The loss of coherence as a system becomes correlated with its environment: off-diagonal terms of the density matrix decay and the state drifts toward a statistical mixture.
The mixed state ρ = e^(−βH)/Tr e^(−βH) of a system in equilibrium at inverse temperature β; at zero temperature it becomes the ground state.
A measure of how close two states are: |⟨φ|ψ⟩|² for pure states, 1 when they are equal and 0 when they are orthogonal. It has a general form for mixed states.
The system with Hamiltonian ħω(a†a + 1/2): evenly spaced levels ħω(n + 1/2). It models a mode of light, a mechanical resonator or a superconducting resonator.
n̂ = a†a, the operator that counts quanta in an oscillator mode; the Fock state |n⟩ is its eigenstate with eigenvalue n.
|0⟩, the oscillator's ground state with no quanta; the annihilation operator sends it to zero. It is also the coherent state with zero amplitude.
A Gaussian state whose uncertainty is pushed below the vacuum level in one quadrature at the cost of more in the other, keeping the uncertainty relation satisfied.
A particle or degree of freedom with two levels, described by the Pauli matrices (S = σ/2 with ħ = 1). Mathematically it is a qubit.
Spins coupled through Z_iZ_j terms, so the energy depends only on whether neighbours align. On its own it is classical (diagonal in the computational basis); a transverse field makes it quantum.
A coupling X_iX_j (often with Y_iY_j, the XY model) that swaps excitations between spins. With only nearest-neighbour terms the chain maps to free fermions.
Spins coupled by X_iX_j + Y_iY_j + Z_iZ_j, which is the same in every direction, so the total spin is conserved.
An interaction only between spins next to each other on a chain or lattice. Hardware with fixed qubit connectivity favours it.
A model with as many independent conserved quantities as degrees of freedom, which makes it exactly solvable and keeps it from thermalising; free-fermion chains are the standard example.
Generic many-body dynamics spreading local information into complicated, many-qubit correlations, so that it can no longer be read from any few-qubit observable.
The state vector (ket) of the system; $\langle\psi\vert$ is its bra and $\vert\psi(t)\rangle$ the state at time $t$.
A second state, as in the inner product $\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle$.
On the Bloch sphere: the azimuthal angle $\phi$ of a qubit state, $0\le\phi<2\pi$, which is the relative phase between $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$.
A phase or rotation angle, as in $\vert0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\vert1\rangle$ or $R_Z(\varphi)$.
The amplitude of $\vert0\rangle$ in a qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$, with $\vert\alpha\vert^2 + \vert\beta\vert^2 = 1$.
For an oscillator: the complex amplitude of a coherent state $\vert\alpha\rangle$, the eigenvalue in $a\vert\alpha\rangle = \alpha\vert\alpha\rangle$; $\vert\alpha\vert^2$ is the mean photon number.
The amplitude of $\vert1\rangle$ in a qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$.
On the Bloch sphere: the polar angle of a qubit state, $\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\vert0\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\vert1\rangle$, so $P(1) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$.
The angle of a rotation gate, $R_P(\theta) = e^{-i\theta P/2}$.
An angle that sets a two-qubit state, as in $\cos\theta\vert00\rangle + \sin\theta\vert11\rangle$.
A global phase: $e^{i\gamma}\vert\psi\rangle$ is the same physical state as $\vert\psi\rangle$.
The amplitude of a basis state in an expansion, most often $c_k = \langle E_k\vert\psi(0)\rangle$ for energy eigenstate $\vert E_k\rangle$, which then evolves as $c_k e^{-iE_kt}$.
The vectors of an orthonormal measurement basis; outcome $k$ has probability $\vert\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2$.
$s$: the input value $s\in[0,1]$ written into a qubit as $\vert\psi_s\rangle = \sqrt{1-s}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{s}\,\vert1\rangle$, the encoding the QRC shelf uses.
$d$: the dimension of a Hilbert space (the number of levels); $d = 2^n$ for $n$ qubits.
$n$: the number of qubits; $n$ qubits need $2^n$ amplitudes.
$n$ (for an oscillator): the number of quanta in the Fock state $\vert n\rangle$, the eigenvalue of $a^\dagger a$.
$\hat n$: a unit vector giving a rotation axis, as in $e^{-i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$.
$\vec r$: the Bloch vector $(\langle X\rangle, \langle Y\rangle, \langle Z\rangle)$; $\vert\vec r\vert = 1$ for a pure state and less for a mixed one.
The number of Trotter steps a time evolution is split into; the first-order error falls as $t^2/r$.
The density matrix, $\rho = \sum_j p_j\vert\psi_j\rangle\langle\psi_j\vert$; $\rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B\rho$ and $\rho_B$ are the reduced density matrices of the two parts.
$p$: a probability: of preparing $\vert\psi_j\rangle$ in a mixture ($p_j$) or of measurement outcome $k$ ($p_k = \operatorname{Tr}(\Pi_k\rho)$).
$p$ (for an oscillator): the momentum quadrature $p = i(a^\dagger - a)/\sqrt2$, with $[x, p] = i$.
$x$ (for an oscillator): the position quadrature $x = (a + a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$.
$H$: the Hamiltonian, the energy observable that generates time evolution, $\vert\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-iHt}\vert\psi(0)\rangle$.
$H_d$: the Hadamard gate, written with a subscript so it is not confused with the Hamiltonian.
A unitary matrix, usually the time-evolution operator $U(t) = e^{-iHt}$.
$I$: the identity matrix (or operator); $I/d$ is the maximally mixed state.
$i$: the imaginary unit, $i^2 = -1$; as a subscript, $i$ labels a qubit (as in $Z_i$).
$X$: the Pauli $X$ matrix, a bit flip; $X_i$ is $X$ acting on qubit $i$.
The Pauli $Y$ matrix; $Y_i$ is $Y$ acting on qubit $i$.
The Pauli $Z$ matrix, diagonal in the computational basis; $Z_i$ acts on qubit $i$ and $\langle Z_i\rangle$ is the usual reservoir feature.
$\vec\sigma = (X, Y, Z)$: the vector of Pauli matrices, so $\rho = \tfrac12(I + \vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$; $\sigma^\pm$ are the raising and lowering operators.

A standard deviation: $\sigma_A$ is the spread of observable $A$'s outcomes, as in $\sigma_A\sigma_B \ge \tfrac12\vert\langle[A,B]\rangle\vert$, and $\sigma(\hat z)$ the shot-noise spread of an estimate.
Rotation gates: $R_P(\theta) = e^{-i\theta P/2}$ turns the Bloch vector by $\theta$ about the $P$ axis.
$P$: a generic Pauli operator, as in $R_P(\theta)$ or $\operatorname{Tr}(PQ) = 2\delta_{PQ}$.
$P$: a probability: $P(0)$, $P(1)$ of a measurement outcome, or $P_1(t)$ of finding the qubit in $\vert1\rangle$ at time $t$.
A conserved quantity: an operator with $[H, Q] = 0$, whose eigenspaces the evolution never mixes.
A second generic Pauli operator, as in $P_iQ_j$.
$S$: the phase gate $S = \mathrm{diag}(1, i)$.
$S$: the number of shots (repetitions) used to estimate an expectation value; the error falls as $1/\sqrt{S}$.
$S$: the entanglement entropy $S = -\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A\log_2\rho_A$.
$\Pi_a$: the projector onto the eigenspace of eigenvalue $a$; outcome $a$ has probability $\Vert\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle\Vert^2$.
The parity operator $\Pi = Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$, conserved by Hamiltonians built from $X_iX_j$ and $Z_i$.
$a$ (for an oscillator): the annihilation operator $a$, which removes one quantum; $a^\dagger$ is the creation operator.
$a$: an eigenvalue label, as in $A = \sum_a a\,\Pi_a$.
$A$: a generic observable or matrix; $A^\dagger$ is its adjoint.
$A$: the first part of a composite system, as in $\rho_A$ and $\vert\psi\rangle_{AB}$.
$B$: a second generic observable or matrix.
$B$: the second part of a composite system, as in $\rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B\rho$.
The energy eigenvalues and eigenstates of $H$; $E_0$ is the ground-state energy.
The eigenvalues of a matrix, as in $A = \sum_k\lambda_k v_kv_k^\dagger$.
The Schmidt coefficients, $\vert\psi\rangle_{AB} = \sum_k\lambda_k\vert a_k\rangle\otimes\vert b_k\rangle$.
The eigenvectors in a spectral decomposition; $V$ is the unitary whose columns they are.
The matrix of eigenvectors in $A = V\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda)\,V^\dagger$.
In QRC: the number of virtual nodes, the times the reservoir is read between two inputs.
$k$: a running index: a basis vector, an eigenvalue, or the input step in QRC.
$t$: time.
The time a reservoir evolves between inputs, $U = e^{-iH\Delta t}$.
The Rabi frequency, the strength of a drive, in $H = \tfrac\delta2 Z + \tfrac\Omega2 X$.
$\delta$: the detuning of a drive from resonance, in $H = \tfrac\delta2 Z + \tfrac\Omega2 X$.
$\delta_{PQ}$: the Kronecker delta, 1 when $P = Q$ and 0 otherwise.
$h$: the field on each spin, the $h_iZ_i$ terms of a spin Hamiltonian ($h$ when it is the same on every spin).
$g$: a field along $x$, the $g_iX_i$ terms of a spin Hamiltonian.
The coupling strength between spins $i$ and $j$ ($J$ when it is uniform).

An energy difference $E_k - E_l$ (divided by $\hbar$), the angular frequency at which an expectation value oscillates when the state is a superposition of the energy eigenstates $\vert E_k\rangle$ and $\vert E_l\rangle$.
The shortest time in which a state can evolve into an orthogonal one, $t_\perp \ge \pi\hbar/(2\Delta E)$, where $\Delta E$ is the state's energy spread (standard deviation).
The equation obeyed by an observable in the Heisenberg picture, $dA_H/dt = i[H, A_H]$ (with $\hbar = 1$): its rate of change is $i$ times its commutator with the Hamiltonian.
A description in between the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures: split $H = H_0 + V$ and follow the motion due to $H_0$ with the frame, so the state moves only under $V_I(t) = e^{iH_0t}Ve^{-iH_0t}$.
In the rotating frame of a driven qubit, the parts of the drive that oscillate at the sum frequency $\omega_0 + \omega$; the rotating-wave approximation drops them.
The amplitudes of a particle's state for every position, $\psi(x) = \langle x\vert\psi\rangle$; $\vert\psi(x)\vert^2$ is the probability density for finding the particle at $x$.
The wavelength $\lambda = h/p$ of a particle with momentum $p$, equivalently $p = \hbar k$; about 1.23 nm for an electron with 1 eV of kinetic energy.
The wavefunction $e^{ikx}$ of definite momentum $p = \hbar k$, spread evenly over all space; it cannot be normalised and is the idealised limit of a very long wave packet.
A wavefunction localised in a region of space, built from a spread of wavelengths; a Gaussian packet of width $\sigma$ has $\Delta x\,\Delta p = \hbar/2$ exactly.
The eigenvalue equation $H\psi = E\psi$ for the energy eigenstates; for a particle it is the differential equation $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi'' + V(x)\psi = E\psi$.
A particle confined between impenetrable walls a distance $L$ apart, with energies $E_n = n^2\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$ and wavefunctions $\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$.

The average energy $\langle\psi\vert H\vert\psi\rangle$ of any normalised trial state is at least the ground-state energy, so lowering it over a family of trial states estimates the ground state from above.

The matrix obtained by putting a wavefunction on a grid of spacing $a$ and replacing $d^2\psi/dx^2$ by $(\psi_{j+1} - 2\psi_j + \psi_{j-1})/a^2$; a particle on $N$ grid points becomes an $N$-level system.
Every continuous symmetry $e^{-i\theta Q}$ of a Hamiltonian has a conserved quantity, its generator $Q$: invariance for all $\theta$ is the same as $[H, Q] = 0$.
The rate of change of an expectation value, $\tfrac{d}{dt}\langle A\rangle = i\langle[H, A]\rangle$ (with $\hbar = 1$, for a time-independent $A$); a zero commutator means a conserved quantity.
The Hermitian operator $Q$ with which a continuous family of symmetries is written $e^{-i\theta Q}$; for rotations of a qubit about $z$ it is $Z/2$.

A symmetry that comes as a single operation rather than a family labelled by an angle, such as a swap of two qubits or the flip $Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$; if its unitary $S$ is also Hermitian, $S$ itself is a conserved observable with eigenvalues $\pm1$.
$M_z = Z_1 + \dots + Z_n$; conserving it is the same as conserving the number of excitations $\sum_i(I - Z_i)/2$.
A Hamiltonian written in a basis sorted by symmetry sector, so that every matrix element between different sectors is zero and each block can be diagonalised on its own.
The lowest energy $\hbar\omega/2$ of a harmonic oscillator; it is not zero because $x$ and $p$ cannot both be sharp.
$[x, p] = i\hbar$, the one quantum ingredient of position and momentum, from which the oscillator's ladder $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$ follows.
The average number of quanta in an oscillator of frequency $f$ at temperature $T$, $\bar n = 1/(e^{hf/k_BT} - 1)$; about $6\times10^{-6}$ for a 5 GHz resonator at 20 mK.
Sending atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field: they land in two separate spots instead of a smear, and magnets in a row show that measuring along $x$ erases what was known along $z$.
The fraction $\cos^2\theta$ of polarised light that passes a polariser turned by $\theta$ from the light's polarisation; for single photons it is a probability.
Crossed polarisers block all light, but a third one at $45^\circ$ placed between them lets $1/8$ of unpolarised light through, because each polariser re-prepares the polarisation.
Two beam splitters and two mirrors that split a beam into two paths and recombine it; with equal paths every photon leaves by one port, a direct demonstration of interference of amplitudes.
An optical element that transmits half the light and reflects half; for a single photon it creates equal amplitudes for the two paths.
Particles sent through two slits build up, one dot at a time, a pattern of bright and dark fringes that adding the one-slit patterns cannot produce.
Amplitudes for indistinguishable alternatives add before squaring, so they can reinforce (constructive) or cancel (destructive); recording which alternative happened removes the effect.

The part $2\,\mathrm{Re}(ab^*)$ of $\vert a + b\vert^2 = \vert a\vert^2 + \vert b\vert^2 + 2\,\mathrm{Re}(ab^*)$ that adding probabilities leaves out; it depends on the phase difference of $a$ and $b$.
A balanced interferometer in which a click at the normally dark detector proves an object blocks one path, though the detected photon never touched it.
The number $i$ with $i^2 = -1$; its powers cycle $i, -1, -i, 1$.
A number $z = a + bi$ with real part $a$ and imaginary part $b$; drawn as an arrow in the complex plane. Quantum amplitudes are complex numbers.
The plane in which $a + bi$ is the point $(a, b)$; addition is adding arrows and multiplication multiplies lengths and adds angles.
$z^* = a - bi$ for $z = a + bi$, the mirror image in the real axis; $zz^* = \vert z\vert^2$.

aliases: absolute value of a complex number
definition: $\vert a + bi\vert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, the length of the arrow; the squared modulus of an amplitude is a probability.
$e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$, which follows from the power series of the exponential, cosine and sine.

aliases: polar form of a complex number
definition: Writing a complex number as $re^{i\theta}$, with length $r = \vert z\vert$ and angle (argument, or phase) $\theta$.
A complex number $e^{i\alpha}$ of modulus 1; multiplying by it turns an amplitude by $\alpha$ without changing its size.
The $N$ solutions $e^{2\pi ik/N}$ of $z^N = 1$, evenly spaced on the unit circle; for $N \ge 2$ they add to zero.
A sum $c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \cdots$ of vectors scaled by numbers; in quantum mechanics a linear combination of states is a superposition.
Vectors whose inner product is zero; orthogonal quantum states can be told apart perfectly by a measurement.
$(AB)_{jk} = \sum_m A_{jm}B_{mk}$: row of the left matrix times column of the right; $AB$ means $B$ acts first, and usually $AB \ne BA$.
$\sum_k f_kf_k^\dagger = I$ for any orthonormal basis $\{f_k\}$: the projectors onto the basis vectors add up to the identity.
$Av = \lambda v$ with $v \ne 0$: the vector $v$ only gets stretched by the matrix $A$, by the factor $\lambda$.
$\det(A - \lambda I)$, a polynomial in $\lambda$ whose roots are the eigenvalues of $A$; for a $2\times2$ matrix it is $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{Tr}A)\lambda + \det A$.
A number $\det A$ computed from a square matrix ($ad - bc$ for rows $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$); it is zero exactly when the matrix has no inverse, and it equals the product of the eigenvalues.

All vectors $v$ with $Av = \lambda v$ for one eigenvalue $\lambda$ (plus the zero vector); for a degenerate eigenvalue it is a plane or larger, and any combination of its vectors is again an eigenvector.
A matrix with zeros everywhere off the main diagonal; its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries and its eigenvectors are the basis vectors.
A square matrix without a full set of independent eigenvectors, such as the one with rows $(0, 1)$ and $(0, 0)$; Hermitian and unitary matrices are never defective.

$f(A) = \sum_k f(\lambda_k)\vert v_k\rangle\langle v_k\vert$ for a Hermitian $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ and eigenvectors $v_k$: apply $f$ to the eigenvalues and keep the eigenvectors. It gives $\sqrt A$, $A^n$ and $e^{-iHt}$.
A matrix with $P^2 = P$, so applying it twice is the same as once; every projector is idempotent and has only the eigenvalues 0 and 1.
A three-level quantum system, with states $\psi_0\vert0\rangle + \psi_1\vert1\rangle + \psi_2\vert2\rangle$ in $\mathbb{C}^3$.
A quantum system with $d$ perfectly distinguishable states, described by unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^d$; a qubit is the case $d = 2$.
The polar angle $\theta$ and azimuth $\varphi$ in $\cos\frac\theta2\vert0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2\vert1\rangle$, which describe every qubit state up to a global phase.
The open question of what physically happens when a measurement gives one definite outcome, as the collapse rule says; interpretations differ but all agree on the predictions.
A projective measurement repeated straight away gives the same outcome with certainty, because the first one left the system in that outcome's basis state.
The standard deviation of an estimate; for the average of $S$ shots of a $\pm1$ observable $A$ it is $\sqrt{(1 - \langle A\rangle^2)/S}$, which is at most $1/\sqrt S$.

An orthonormal basis whose vectors are eigenvectors of two or more operators at once. Hermitian operators have one exactly when they commute, and then one measurement in that basis gives all their values.

Observables whose operators do not commute. They have no complete set of shared eigenvectors, so no state is sharp in both, measuring one disturbs the other, and the order of measuring them changes the statistics.

For any two vectors, $\vert\langle f\vert g\rangle\vert^2 \le \langle f\vert f\rangle\langle g\vert g\rangle$: an overlap never exceeds the product of the lengths. It is the key step in deriving the uncertainty relation.

A strengthened uncertainty relation that adds a covariance term to Robertson's bound: $\sigma_A^2\sigma_B^2 \ge \vert\tfrac12\langle[A, B]\rangle\vert^2 + (\tfrac12\langle\{A, B\}\rangle - \langle A\rangle\langle B\rangle)^2$.
The observable for a particle's momentum; acting on a wavefunction it differentiates, $p\,\psi = -i\hbar\,d\psi/dx$.
The observable for a particle's position; acting on a wavefunction it multiplies by the coordinate, $x\,\psi(x)$.
An observable has a sharp value in a state when every measurement of it gives the same result, which happens exactly when the state is an eigenvector of the observable (zero variance).
An operator $K$ with $K^\dagger = -K$. The commutator of two Hermitian operators is anti-Hermitian, so $i[A, B]$ is Hermitian and $\langle[A, B]\rangle$ is purely imaginary.

A state in which the uncertainty relation holds with equality, $\sigma_A\sigma_B = \tfrac12\vert\langle[A, B]\rangle\vert$. For position and momentum these are the Gaussian wave packets, such as the oscillator ground state.

The orthonormal basis of the four two-qubit Bell states $(\vert00\rangle \pm \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $(\vert01\rangle \pm \vert10\rangle)/\sqrt2$. It is the shared eigenbasis of the commuting parities $Z_1Z_2$ and $X_1X_2$, whose four sign pairs label the four states.

An observable such as $Z_1Z_2$ that reports $+1$ when two qubits agree and $-1$ when they differ, without revealing either qubit's own value. Its eigenvalues are degenerate, so measuring it does not tell $\vert00\rangle$ from $\vert11\rangle$.
The six qubit states on the axes of the Bloch sphere: $\vert0\rangle$, $\vert1\rangle$, $\vert{\pm}\rangle$ and $\vert{\pm i}\rangle$, the eigenstates of $Z$, $X$ and $Y$.
The Pauli $X$ gate, which swaps $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$ (and so swaps the two amplitudes of any state); a half turn of the Bloch sphere about the $x$ axis.
The Pauli $Z$ gate, which leaves $\vert0\rangle$ alone and multiplies $\vert1\rangle$ by $-1$; it turns $\vert{+}\rangle$ into $\vert{-}\rangle$, a half turn about the $z$ axis.

Writing a $2\times2$ matrix $M$ as $a_0I + a_1X + a_2Y + a_3Z$ with each coefficient $\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(MP)$ for the matching $P \in \{I, X, Y, Z\}$; the coefficients are real exactly when the matrix is Hermitian.
Every single-qubit gate can be written $U = e^{i\alpha}R_Z(\beta)R_Y(\gamma)R_Z(\delta)$: a global phase and three rotations about two fixed axes.
An object, such as the state of a spin-1/2 particle or a qubit, that a $360°$ rotation multiplies by $-1$; it takes $720°$ to bring it back exactly. The sign is visible in interference.
The rise and fall of a detector's count rate as the phase difference between two paths is changed; in a Mach–Zehnder interferometer $P(\mathrm{D0}) = \cos^2(\varphi/2)$.

$V = (P_{\max} - P_{\min})/(P_{\max} + P_{\min})$, how strongly a fringe swings: 1 for perfect interference, 0 for none. When a which-path record is the only imperfection, it equals the overlap of the record states.
An element that delays one path of an interferometer, multiplying its amplitude by $e^{i\varphi}$; on the path qubit it is the gate $\mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\varphi})$.

Any record, read or not, of which route a particle took; it reduces interference to the overlap $\vert\langle m_0\vert m_1\rangle\vert$ of the record states and removes it completely when they are orthogonal.
Measuring a which-path record in a basis that reveals nothing about the path; sorting the runs by that result brings back the fringe in each group, while the overall statistics never change.

Feeding an oracle's target qubit the state $\vert{-}\rangle$ turns $U_f\vert x\rangle\vert{-}\rangle$ into $(-1)^{f(x)}\vert x\rangle\vert{-}\rangle$: the function value becomes a phase on the control register.
A gate that evaluates a function reversibly, $U_f\vert x\rangle\vert y\rangle = \vert x\rangle\vert y\oplus f(x)\rangle$; algorithms are compared by how many times they must call it.

A one-query quantum procedure that decides whether $f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$ is constant or balanced, which classically needs two queries; it reads the relative phase $(-1)^{f(0)}$ versus $(-1)^{f(1)}$ by interference.
A function on bit strings that outputs 0 on exactly half its inputs and 1 on the other half; Deutsch's problem asks whether a function is balanced or constant.
The single-qubit gate $\mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\pi/4})$, an eighth of a turn about the $z$ axis of the Bloch sphere; added to $H_d$ and CNOT it makes a gate set that can approximate any unitary.

The number of time steps a circuit takes when gates on different qubits run in parallel: group the gates into layers in which no qubit is used twice and count the layers. It sets how long the qubits must survive.
A measurement that asks which of the four Bell states two qubits are in; in a circuit it is a CNOT, then $H_d$ on the control, then a measurement of both qubits in the $Z$ basis.

The symmetric step $e^{-iBt/2r}e^{-iAt/r}e^{-iBt/2r}$ for approximating $e^{-i(A+B)t}$; its total error falls as $1/r^2$ in the number of steps $r$, instead of $1/r$ for the plain first-order product.
The gates generated by $H_d$, $S$ and CNOT, which map Pauli operators to Pauli operators; circuits made only of them can be simulated efficiently on an ordinary computer and are not universal.
The result that a circuit of Clifford gates acting on $\vert0\ldots0\rangle$, followed by measurements in the $Z$ basis, can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.

The theorem that a finite universal gate set such as $\{H_d, T, \mathrm{CNOT}\}$ approximates any single-qubit gate to accuracy $\varepsilon$ with a number of gates that grows only like a power of $\log(1/\varepsilon)$.

The steady turning of a qubit's Bloch vector about the field axis under $H_0 = (\omega_0/2)Z$, at the angular frequency $\omega_0$ (the Larmor frequency); the populations of $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$ never change.
The constant $\gamma$ linking a spin's precession frequency to the magnetic field, $\omega_0 = \gamma B$; for a proton $\gamma/2\pi \approx 42.58$ MHz per tesla.

A description of a driven qubit that turns about $z$ at the drive frequency, $\vert\tilde\psi\rangle = e^{i\omega_d tZ/2}\vert\psi\rangle$; it removes the fast precession, leaves populations unchanged, and makes a resonant drive look static.

Dropping the part of a drive that, in the rotating frame, spins at twice the drive frequency, because it averages to almost nothing; it leaves the constant Hamiltonian $\tfrac\delta2 Z + \tfrac\Omega2(X\cos\phi + Y\sin\phi)$.
$W = \sqrt{\Omega^2 + \delta^2}$, the rate at which a detuned drive rotates the Bloch vector; off resonance the population oscillates at $W$ rather than at the Rabi frequency $\Omega$.

$P_1(t) = \frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\delta^2}\sin^2(\sqrt{\Omega^2+\delta^2}\,t/2)$, the probability that a qubit starting in $\vert0\rangle$ is in $\vert1\rangle$ after a drive of strength $\Omega$ and detuning $\delta$ has been on for a time $t$.
A resonant drive whose pulse area is $\pi$, so it rotates the Bloch vector by half a turn about an axis in the $xy$ plane; about $x$ it is the NOT gate $R_X(\pi) = -iX$.
A resonant drive with pulse area $\pi/2$, a quarter turn about an axis in the $xy$ plane; it takes $\vert0\rangle$ to an equal superposition on the equator of the Bloch sphere.
The integral $\int\Omega(t)\,dt$ of a resonant drive's Rabi frequency over the pulse; it equals the rotation angle, whatever the pulse shape.
A rotation about $z$ made by shifting the phase of every later drive pulse instead of applying a pulse; it is exact and takes no time.

Two $\pi/2$ pulses separated by a free wait $\tau$; the final population $P_1 = \cos^2(\delta\tau/2)$ oscillates with $\tau$, which measures the detuning $\delta$ precisely, and the fringes fade at the dephasing time.
The small shift, of order $\Omega^2/\omega_0$, of a driven qubit's resonance caused by the counter-rotating terms that the rotating-wave approximation drops.
A shaped drive pulse with a correction on the other quadrature that suppresses leakage of a transmon out of its two lowest levels (Motzoi et al. 2009).
